summary:
Quindío department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Entry, partner recognition and family law are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and to detention is governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The formal framework sits alongside lethal anti-trans violence that is carried out in daylight, filmed and left unpunished. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, showing her unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before she drowned, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, but police questioned local residents and no one was arrested. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and 41 trans women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Caquetá department, flyers on the street and circulated via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets in a declared "social cleansing"; three armed men gave a trans woman and local election candidate one week to leave town, she hid for a week and then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond hairdressing and sex work. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

The sources assembled for Quindío report no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework plus the pattern of territorial violence documented elsewhere in Colombia, which is the risk a trans visitor to Quindío should expect to encounter rather than a Quindío case record.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's formal protections and its lethal violence are not in tension so much as concurrent: the same period that produced the notary-based marker change and the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" document markers also produced 13 trans hate killings in a single quarter and a filmed daylight assault in which no arrest followed a presidential order.

The documented killings and forced departures are concentrated in departments with a persistent armed-group presence rather than in Quindío, notably Antioquia, Caquetá and Guajira. Reporting characterises the brutality as calculated and as continuing amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, which places any urban visit inside a wider pattern of territorial armed actors rather than ordinary street crime.

Colombia's framework compares favourably with most of Latin America on paper, and the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission both praised the reforms and warned of a gap between institutional progress and lived experience. That gap, not the statute book, is the operative variable for a visitor.

Discrimination narrows trans women's livelihood options to hairdressing or sex work in the departments surveyed, and armed-group kill lists published since March 2024 explicitly name trans people as military targets. Both conditions raise the cost of being visibly trans in public for any length of time.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory makes a Quindío-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. The Millerey killing is recorded in Bello, Antioquia, and the organised flyer campaigns in Caquetá and Guajira; neither EL PAÍS nor The Guardian reports a Quindío case, arrest, or complaint.

Whether Quindío's own police, prosecutors or courts have handled a trans-specific case is not sourced here and remains unresolved. The same applies to any Quindío-local facility, restroom or detention complaint; the facilities judgments cited (Tequendama Hotel, Cosmocentro in Cali, the Santa Marta boardwalk) arise in other departments.

The status of the two trans women displaced in Caquetá after the July 2024 reporting, and whether any arrest has followed the Millerey investigation since the April 2025 article, are unresolved on this inventory. The figures of 13 trans killings in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 and 41 trans killings in 2023 come from different counting bodies and are not reconciled with one another here.
